title: Impact of inverse relationship between TP53 and CARF on the development of hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance
text:
The increasing prevalence of insulin resistance (IR) and non-alcoholic fatty liver diseases (NAFLD) in the USA requires
continued effort to define underlying mechanisms and identify new drug targets. This project will investigate the causative
role of P53-CARF interplay in IR and NAFLD and establish that understanding its function will help manage IR and
NAFLD.

title: Vet-LIRN Network Capacity-Building Project: Bacterial Whole Genome Sequencing
text:
Antimicrobial resistance in bacteria has become a significant concern in human health. The lack
of antimicrobial stewardship and increased use of antimicrobial drugs in animal feeds has led to
the emergence of antibiotic-resistant bacterial pathogens from companion and food-producing
animals. The availability of benchtop DNA sequencing platforms provides an accurate whole-
genome sequence (WGS) for a broad range of bacteria in less than a day. Thus, identifying
genetic determinants of antimicrobial resistance and typing of clinically critical bacterial pathogens
help accurately define the transmission of drug-resistant and multi-drug-resistant organisms. The
work performed under this project will allow a continuing collaboration with Center for Veterinary
Medicine’s Vet-LIRN into investigating of human and animal food safety using Whole Genome
Sequencing (WGS).

title: Comprehensive NeuroHIV Center
text:
The overall goal of the Comprehensive NeuroHIV Center (CNHC) is to develop, improve and sustain an
infrastructure to provide services to a large number of scientists from the Philadelphia and beyone are who are
involved in high impact research towards neuroHIV. CNHC offers unique expertise and services in gene editing
strategies and delivery, cellular neurobiology and functional assessments and neuropsychological, virological
and immunological data within a well-characterized and longitudinal clinical cohort. CNHC will provide pilot
funding for junior investigators to enhance training and research for the next generation HIV scientists.

title: Deciphering molecular mechanisms controlling age-associated uterine adaptabilityto pregnancy
text:
A prominent alteration in the uterine environment has recently been identified as a prevalent cause of age-related
reproductive decline independent of blastocyst aneuploidy. This problem is likely due to a blunted progesterone
(P4) responsiveness of the aging uterus, via its cognate nuclear receptor PGR. The goal of this proposal is to
investigate the molecular mechanisms that underlie the age-associated uterine adaptability to pregnancy using
physiological and genetic aging mouse models at single cell resolution.

title: Genetic Analysis of Cryptosporidium
text:
Cryptosporidium is one of the most important causes of diarrheal disease in
the U.S. and around the world. This project will reveal the mechanisms that underlie parasite
persistence and host specificity.

title: DNA Nanostructures for High-Throughput Cryo-EM Studies of Small Macromolecules
text:
Macromolecules play key roles in nearly all biological processes, and thus understanding their
structure and function is critical to human health. Determining structures of macromolecules would be
highly beneficial for elucidating mechanisms of human disease and designing countermeasures.
Despite recent advances, many health-relevant macromolecules remain difficult to study. We propose
to use DNA nanotechnology to gain programmable spatial control over these targets to their enable
structure determination.

title: Project 02: Cancer Control (CC)
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – CANCER CONTROL (CC) The Cancer Control (CC) Program at The Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center (OSUCCC), led by Theodore Wagener, PhD, Diane Von Ah, PhD, and Jesse Plascak, PhD has 62 members from six OSU Colleges (Arts & Sciences, Law, Medicine, Nursing, Public Health, and Social Work). The overall goal of the CC Program is to conduct research to reduce the incidence, mortality, and morbidity of cancer in our catchment area (CA)—the state of Ohio—and beyond. The CC Program conducts research across the cancer control continuum, from etiology through survivorship, and across the lifespan. Crosscutting themes unite the aims of the program and include policy and populations with poor outcomes, with a focus on the priority cancers of the OSUCCC. Our research also capitalizes on our members’ strengths, such as epidemiology, biology, nursing, and behavior, and includes transdisciplinary research teams. The Specific Aims of the CC Program are to: 1) Identify molecular, genetic, behavioral and contextual factors related to cancer incidence and mortality at a population level; 2) Develop and test behavioral interventions that prevent cancer development or facilitate early detection; and 3) Assess and intervene on issues of cancer survivorship (including patients on active cancer treatment and survivors). CC Program members published 1,635 cancer-relevant manuscripts between (7/1/2019 - 6/30/2024). Of these, 26% were intra-programmatic (multiple authors from CC Program), 31% were inter-programmatic (authors from multiple OSUCCC Programs), and 90% were multi-institutional (authors from both CC and another institution). CC Program funding stands at $14.9M in overall direct, cancer-focused funding, of which $12.4M is peer-reviewed, including $11.5M direct funding from NIH ($9.1M from NCI). Over the last 5 years, CC Program members have accrued 31,844 participants to studies: 9,863 to interventional trials (non-therapeutic/ therapeutic) and 21,981 to non-interventional studies. Future plans for the CC Program include expanding research in 1) molecular epidemiology; 2) obesity, diet, and physical activity, and 3) survivorship, including the role of social and built environment factors, the effects of immuno-oncology on patient outcomes and immune related adverse events through collaborations with the Pelotonia Institute for Immuno-Oncology (PIIO), and the impact of psychedelic-assisted therapy on the treatment of cancer-related depression, anxiety, and quality of life. We also integrate with the new Center for Cancer Prevention and Survivorship (CCPS) that will bring together transdisciplinary teams of researchers across the OSUCCC to focus on cancer prevention and survivorship with a multi-level focus and innovative design strategies.

title: Multimodal and Generative AI for Pathology
text:
This project involves the development of deep learning-based algorithms for pathology image analysis. The
renewal of this grant will enable us to continue the development of open-source methods and software for
microscopy image analysis that will enable basic and applied research in biomedicine.

title: PHAGE IMMUNOPRECIPITATION SEQUENCING (PhIP-SEQ) TO IDENTIFY AUTOANTIBODIES FROM PARTICIPANTS FROM THE SJÖGREN’S INTERNATIONAL COLLABORATIVE CLINICAL ALLIANCE (SICCA)
text:
Our project seeks to improve the diagnosis and possible treatment of Sjögren’s Disease, an autoimmune
condition that predominantly affects women and often leads to severe dry eye disease. By using advanced
genetic sequencing technologies, we aim to identify specific markers in tears that can diagnose this disease
more accurately and earlier. This could lead to better treatment options that enhance health, extend life, and
reduce the burden of this disabling condition, thereby significantly improving the quality of life for patients with
Sjögren’s Disease, particularly women.

title: Unraveling molecular Complexity of Mitral Valve Disease using single cell and Spatial Multi-Omics analysis"
text:
Myxomatous mitral valve prolapse, a potentially life-threatening heart valve condition, specifically affects the valve
located between the left atrium and ventricle. Despite some reports on the intricate cellular environments involved,
there is a notable scarcity of detailed high-resolution omics data. The objective of this project is to bridge this
knowledge gap by utilizing state-of-the-art single-cell and spatial techniques to construct a comprehensive
molecular atlas of the tissue affected by mitral valve prolapse.

title: TissueReM: Whole-Organism, Real-time Decision-enabled 3D Tissue Imaging and Recovery for Molecular Analysis
text:
Narrative. We will further refine AI-driven, deep-learning software for automatically identifying organs/tissues
and classifying them as healthy versus diseased using CryoVizTM Imaging. Downstream analysis will include AI-
based, “virtually stained” images from scanned images of label-free sections, and 3D registration so that tissue-
of-interest can be collected, processed, and registered back to the block-face imaging data, enabling correlation
of histology at a cellular/sub-cellular level with block-face images at the organ/tissue level. It will serve a wide
variety of application areas including cancer therapeutics, cell-based immunotherapy, drug delivery, imaging
agents and gene expression.

title: Control of regulatory T cell fitness and function by heme synthesis
text:
Autoimmune diseases often involve dysfunctional Foxp3+ regulatory T (Treg) cells, leading to harmful immune
responses. This project explores the role of heme synthesis in regulating Treg fitness and function, with the goal
of identifying new therapeutic strategies to restore Treg function in autoimmunity. By investigating how heme
synthesis influences Treg stability and suppressive capabilities, and identifying regulatory mechanisms that
control this pathway, the findings may offer novel approaches to improve Treg-based therapies for autoimmune
diseases.

title: Research Specialist in Cancer Genomics to Integrate Basic Research and Clinical Data
text:
The analyses of cancer genomes have provided remarkable insights into the origin of cancer and exposed
features that have been leveraged for prevention and treatment. This proposal will provide support for a scientist
skilled in laboratory and computational genomics to engage a range of translational researchers developing
approaches to improve cancer outcomes.

title: Delivering inhalable nanoparticles containing AI-optimized CFTR mRNA with a novel microfluidic device for treatment of CF
text:
Cystic fibrosis is a pulmonary disease caused by mutations in the CFTR gene. One promising therapeutic
approach is delivering CFTR mRNA to lung cells in small nanoparticles but the current technology for airway
delivery and the CFTR mRNA sequence design has not been clinically effective. We propose using state-of-
the-art nebulizer technology for nanoparticle airway delivery and computationally-assisted design to improve
mRNA therapies for treating cystic fibrosis.

title: Project 2: Validating and Characterizing Subtype-Specific AD Therapeutic Targets in Human Brains and iPSC Models
text: Project 2: Target Validation Here we aim to validate and refine therapeutic targets for Alzheimer’s disease (AD) subtypes by investigating the functional roles of prioritized genes and proteins identified in prior research and that emerge from Project 1 multi-scale subtypes. The central hypothesis is that distinct biological domains are altered in each subtype of aging brains, requiring therapeutic strategies tailored to subtype-specific hub genes within specific cell types. By integrating spatial and cellular characterization of targets in human brains with genetic and chemical screens in iPSC-derived brain cell models, this project addresses both subtypespecific and shared disease mechanisms in AD. These efforts will identify and prioritize the cellular and molecular pathways driving distinct AD pathologies. The project is organized into three aims. Aim 1 employs advanced imaging and molecular profiling to map the spatial and cellular relationships of target proteins in AD brains from multiple well-characterized longitudinal cohorts, linking them to hallmark pathologies such as amyloid plaques and tau tangles. Aim 2 utilizes CRISPR screens and single-cell profiling to systematically characterize the functional roles of candidate genes in neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, uncovering regulatory networks driving AD pathology in specific subtypes. Finally, Aim 3 examines the impact of genetic and pharmacological perturbations on multi-cellular human models, focusing on key diseaserelevant outcomes, including synaptic integrity, neuroinflammation, and lipid homeostasis. Together, these approaches will refine therapeutic targets, provide deeper insights into the biological mechanisms underlying AD subtypes, and advance personalized therapeutic strategies.

title: Elucidating neuron-astrocyte mechanisms underlying ultrasound stimulation for Alzheimer's disease
text:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia in nearly 7 million individuals, exceeding $360
billion in healthcare costs as of 2024. As current treatments offer limited clinical benefit, disrupted
communication between neurons and astrocytes has emerged as a critical driver of cognitive decline in AD.
This project will determine whether low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) can mitigate neuron-astrocyte
dysfunction and improves cognition, advancing the development of non-invasive approaches for AD and
related neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, epilepsy, and stroke.

title: Mindfulness-based ecological momentary intervention for smoking cessation among cancer survivors
text:
Continued tobacco use among cancer survivors is a cause of second primary cancers and increased overall
mortality, thus, there is an urgent need to develop novel smoking cessation interventions that particularly target
cancer-specific risk factors of smoking relapse in real-time given chronic levels of high stress and unique
cessation barriers in this population. We propose to develop a mindfulness-based intervention for smoking
cessation tailored for cancer survivors, that delivers intervention content via smartphone application in real-time
when risk of smoking relapse is high. This project will result in a highly scalable and cost-effective intervention
for cancer survivors ready to be tested in a large-scale clinical trial.

title: Maturation of frontal cortico-thalamic circuitry in control of social behavior
text:
This study aims to identify the developmental mechanisms and windows when a frontal circuit projecting to
thalamus, which is responsible for social processing, are sensitive to modulation by aberrant social experience
or genetic risk of neurodevelopmental disorders. Such information will point toward therapeutic targets that allow
amelioration of social deficits.

title: Cohesin independent co-function of BRD4 and NIPBL in regulating chromatin and transcription factor genome occupancy
text:
Enhancers are distal DNA regulatory elements that drive gene expression during crucial cell state transitions.
Chromatin factors that bind and regulate enhancers play a key role in development and disease as mutations
in these chromatin modifiers promote various craniofacial disorders. Gaining a comprehensive understanding
of where these enhancer-binding chromatin factors localize, their target genes, and their mechanisms of action
will be instrumental in elucidating the pathogenic mechanisms and developing therapeutic strategies for
chromatin based disorders.

title: Role of a craniosynostosis associated fibroblast growth factor receptor mutation in extraocular muscles
text:
Apert syndrome is a devastating genetic syndrome with abnormal skull development and strabismus, or
eye misalignment. This research proposal will use a model for Apert syndrome to examine why patients have
abnormal muscles around the eye and what might be causing their abnormal vision using state-of-the-art
techniques in muscle biomechanics and genetics. Gene therapy will also be tested using this model to investigate
innovative therapies for patients with strabismus in Apert syndrome.
